newsitem.title: USA: Astronaut Hall of Fame ends rift with space widows.
newsitem.headline: Astronaut Hall of Fame ends rift with space widows.

text.p: Officials at the Astronaut Hall of Fame said on Wednesday they would admit Apollo 1 astronaut Roger Chaffee, settling a dispute that threatened to tear apart the tight-knit U.S. astronaut community.
"I'm very relieved," said Chaffee's widow, Martha. "I'm just very happy and very relieved that they did the right thing."

Chaffee, Gus Grissom and Ed White died on a launch pad in January 1967 when fire swept through their sealed and pressurized spacecraft during a countdown rehearsal before Chaffee was to have made his first space flight.

On May 5, adhering to a requirement that the Hall of Fame be limited to astronauts who had been in space, its board voted down a proposal by Grissom's widow, Betty, to admit Chaffee along with other Apollo astronauts this October.

Both Grissom and White had flown before the ill-fated Apollo 1 mission. Grissom, the Apollo 1 commander, was the second American to fly in space, is already in the Hall. White was the first American to walk in space.
Mrs. Grissom, who served on the Hall's board in her husband's place, quit and threatened to have her husband's personal belongings removed from Hall displays after the vote to exclude Chaffee.
"I just felt it was a slap in the face to the whole crew of Apollo 1," Grissom told Reuters. "For 30 years, NASA and the astronaut corps have tried to pretend that fire never happened."

Grissom said that the heated space race between the United States and the Soviet Union -- the prize was putting a man on the moon -- caused NASA to conduct a hurried and slipshod investigation into the Apollo 1 deaths.
As a result, she said, NASA never gave the fallen crewmen the recognition they deserved.

Howard Benedict, execution director of the foundation that operates the non-profit Hall of Fame, said the issue of Chaffee's induction reignited some jealousies and resentments that had long been part of the astronaut community.
"None of us really understood why Betty reacted the way she did. It's probably like a family where old issues just keep coming back," he said.

The board changed its policy after Hall of Fame astronaut Gene Cernan, the last man to walk on the moon, pressed for a compromise under which Chaffee, an Air Force pilot who flew U-2s over Soviet missile bases during the Cuban Missile Crisis, will be admitted to the hall for his "significant contribution to the space programme."
Cernan argued that future Apollo missions were made safer by Chaffee's sacrifice.

The compromise did not address the thorny issue of Christa McAuliffe, Mike Smith and Greg Jarvis, who had never flown in space when they died in the 1986 Challenger explosion. That accident, which took the lives of all seven astronauts on board, took place before the shuttle left the Earth's atmosphere.
Benedict said that all astronauts who served after Project Apollo ended in 1972 will be evaluated on a case-by-case basis by an independent commission.
